title: LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE
path: MATH 2ND YEAR/MATH 2303/LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE.md
body:
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) taught the machinery: [[Matrix|matrices]],
[[Determinant|determinants]], [[Basis|bases]], [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors|eigenvalues]]. This
course points all of it at data, and the change of emphasis is total. Square invertible matrices
with exact solutions give way to tall rectangular ones with no solution at all, because a dataset
has more rows than parameters and the rows disagree. Everything here is an answer to that
situation: [[Projection]] instead of solving, [[Least Squares]] instead of $A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$,
[[Singular Value Decomposition|SVD]] instead of [[Diagonalization]], approximation instead of
equality. The course profile puts algorithms run on real datasets ahead of theory, and block 6 is
two hours a week of [[NumPy]] doing exactly that.

**It is also the keystone of this degree's mathematics.** It is the only place
[[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]], the SVD, and norms-as-loss-functions live, and the chain
[[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] → [[Spectral Theorem]] → [[Singular Value Decomposition]] →
[[Principal Component Analysis]] is the route from the MATH block into [[MACHINE LEARNING]]. Two
courses hand material here without owning it: MATH 1203's eigenvalues arrive at PCA, and
[[STATISTICS]]'s regression is [[Least Squares]] seen from the other side.

The single organising idea, if you keep one: **when the system has no solution, project.** The
closest point of a subspace is a [[Projection]], the residual is orthogonal to it, and that one
picture is [[Least Squares]], PCA, [[Gram-Schmidt]], compression, and Fourier coefficients, all of
them.

## Topics

### Inner product spaces and orthogonality

- [[Inner Product]]: the [[Dot Product]] with the formula thrown away and the three rules kept,
  so length, angle, and orthogonality transfer to matrices and to functions
- [[Projection]]: dropping a vector onto a subspace, the orthogonal decomposition into fit plus
  residual, and the projection matrix $P = A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$. **The geometric spine of the course**
- [[Orthonormal Basis]]: why orthogonality is worth paying for (coordinates by dot product, and
  coefficients you can truncate), and orthogonal matrices with $Q^{-1} = Q^T$
- [[Gram-Schmidt]]: manufacturing an orthonormal basis by subtracting off projections, and the
  QR decomposition that falls out of bookkeeping it
- [[Vector Norm]]: $L_1$, $L_2$, $L_\infty$, Frobenius, the metric each one induces, and
  **norms as loss functions**, which is where this course meets model training

### Spectral theory

- [[Spectral Theorem]]: symmetric matrices diagonalise orthogonally, $A = QDQ^T$, with real
  eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, and it never fails. The matrices data produces
  (covariance, Gram, adjacency, Hessian) are symmetric almost by construction
- [[Quadratic Form]]: $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$, positive and negative definiteness read off the
  eigenvalue signs, the principal axes theorem, and the Hessian test for a multivariable
  maximum, minimum, or saddle

### Singular value decomposition

- [[Singular Value Decomposition]]: $A = U\Sigma V^T$ for **every** matrix, square or not,
  singular or not. The [[Spectral Theorem]] applied once on each side
- The geometry: every linear map is a rotation, a stretch, and another rotation, and the image of
  the unit sphere is an ellipsoid with the singular values as its semi-axes
- [[Low-Rank Approximation]]: truncate the sum of rank-one terms. Eckart-Young-Mirsky says the
  result is **provably the best** approximation of that rank, with error equal to the discarded
  tail
- [[Principal Component Analysis]]: the covariance matrix's eigenvectors are the directions of
  greatest variance, keep the top $k$ and project. Maximising retained variance and minimising
  reconstruction error turn out to be the same optimisation

### Transforms and signal approximation

- The [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] turns a data vector into a frequency signature, and it is
  introduced here as a change of basis on data. [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) owns
  the transform itself and the [[Fast Fourier Transform]]; this course only borrows it
- [[Wavelet Transform]]: a localised basis, so a coefficient says *how much* and *where* rather
  than just how much. Multi-resolution analysis, and why modern compression uses it
- [[Image Processing]]: an image is a [[Matrix]], filtering is convolution is a [[Dot Product]],
  edge detection is differentiation, and compression is a truncated SVD you can look at

### Numerical linear algebra

- [[Pseudoinverse]]: Moore-Penrose $A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^T$, which exists for every matrix and returns
  the exact solution, the least squares fit, or the minimum-norm one, depending on what the system
  admits
- [[Least Squares]]: the geometric derivation. The reachable set is a column space, the closest
  point is a [[Projection]], so the residual is orthogonal and the normal equations
  $A^TA\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^T\mathbf{b}$ follow with no calculus at all

### Applied computing laboratory

- [[NumPy]]: `svd`, `eigh`, `qr`, `lstsq`, `pinv`, `norm`, and the two habits the lab teaches that
  the theory does not (never call `inv`, and vectorise)

## Core Facts to Know

- **When $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has no solution, project $\mathbf{b}$ onto the column space.**
  Every algorithm in this course is that sentence somewhere.
- Every vector splits uniquely into a component in a subspace $W$ and a component in $W^\perp$.
  The projection is the **closest point of $W$**, and the residual is orthogonal to all of $W$.
- $\text{proj}_W\mathbf{v} = \sum_i (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i)\mathbf{u}_i$ **only for an
  orthonormal basis.** For a general basis use $P = A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$.
- A projection matrix is exactly one that is idempotent ($P^2 = P$) and symmetric ($P^T = P$). Its
  eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$, $\text{rank}(P) = \text{tr}(P)$, and $I - P$ projects onto $W^\perp$.
- In an [[Orthonormal Basis]] coordinates are one [[Dot Product]] each instead of an $O(n^3)$
  solve, and **truncating the coefficients is meaningful**. In a skewed basis it is not.
- $Q$ orthogonal means $Q^{-1} = Q^T$, lengths and angles preserved, $\det Q = \pm 1$. Rotations
  and reflections, nothing else.
- $L_2$ is the only norm that comes from an [[Inner Product]]. That is why it alone has a
  projection formula, a closed-form solution, and a smooth gradient.
- **$L_2$ squared is mean squared error, $L_1$ is mean absolute error.** MSE squares outliers so
  they dominate; MAE is robust and has no closed form. As a penalty on the weights, $L_2$ (ridge)
  shrinks smoothly and $L_1$ (lasso) drives coefficients to exactly zero.
- $\|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2} = \sqrt{\sum_k \sigma_k^2}$, and $\|A\|_2 = \sigma_1$.
- **Spectral theorem: orthogonally diagonalizable $\iff$ symmetric.** Real eigenvalues, orthogonal
  eigenvectors, and it never fails, unlike ordinary [[Diagonalization]].
- $A = \sum_i \lambda_i \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T$: a symmetric matrix is a weighted sum of
  rank-one projections.
- **Any $A^TA$ is symmetric positive semidefinite**, so $\mathbf{x}^TA^TA\mathbf{x} =
  \|A\mathbf{x}\|^2 \geq 0$ and its eigenvalues are non-negative. Their square roots are the
  singular values of $A$.
- Definiteness is the sign pattern of the eigenvalues: all positive is a minimum, all negative a
  maximum, mixed is a saddle. Applied to the Hessian that is the multivariable second-derivative
  test.
- **Every matrix has an SVD.** $A = U\Sigma V^T$ with $U, V$ orthogonal and
  $\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0$. Rectangular, singular, and defective are all fine.
- $A\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i$: the eigenvector equation with the input and output
  directions allowed to differ, which is why it works on non-square matrices.
- $V$ holds the eigenvectors of $A^TA$, $U$ those of $AA^T$, and $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$.
- Every linear map is **rotate, stretch, rotate**. The unit sphere maps to an ellipsoid with
  semi-axes $\sigma_i$.
- $A = \sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{v}_i^T$, where $r$ is the rank. The SVD hands you
  orthonormal bases for all four fundamental subspaces, and numerical rank is a count of singular
  values above a tolerance.
- Condition number $\sigma_1/\sigma_r$ says how much error gets amplified. The [[Determinant]]
  cannot see it.
- **Eckart-Young-Mirsky: the truncated SVD $A_k$ is the best rank-$k$ approximation there is**, in
  both the Frobenius and spectral norms, with $\|A - A_k\|_F = \sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \cdots}$ and
  $\|A - A_k\|_2 = \sigma_{k+1}$.
- Truncation compresses because **real data has fast-decaying singular values**: correlated
  columns mean near-dependence means small $\sigma_i$.
- **PCA: centre, covariance, eigen-decompose, keep the top $k$, project.** Centring is not
  optional. In practice take the SVD of the centred matrix instead of forming the covariance.
- The data matrix $X$ is $n \times p$, **samples in rows**, the one place this vault departs from
  columns-as-vectors. So covariance is $X_c^TX_c$ and the components are the **right** singular
  vectors. Transposing the convention transposes every formula.
- Principal components are **uncorrelated by construction**, being orthogonal eigenvectors of the
  covariance matrix. Maximising retained variance and minimising reconstruction error are one
  optimisation.
- PCA is scale sensitive (standardise first), linear (no curved manifolds), and unsupervised (it
  never looks at the labels). Variance is not the same as usefulness.
- **Normal equations: $A^TA\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^T\mathbf{b}$.** "Normal" means perpendicular.
  Derived from orthogonality of the residual, with no calculus.
- Least squares and statistical regression are the **same equations twice**: $\text{SSR} =
  \|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2$, the fitted values are a projection of the observed, and $R^2$ is Pythagoras.
- A regression model only has to be **linear in the coefficients**. Columns of $x^2$ or $\log x$
  fit curves with the same machinery.
- Do not form $A^TA$ numerically: it squares the condition number. Use QR, or the SVD when the
  matrix is rank deficient.
- $A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^T$, inverting the non-zero singular values and leaving the zeros alone. It
  gives $A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, the least squares fit, or the minimum-norm solution, whichever the
  system admits. $AA^+ = P$.
- Filtering an image is convolution, a [[Dot Product]] of a kernel with a patch. A Sobel kernel is
  a discrete derivative, so **edge detection is differentiation**, and a [[CNN]] learns these
  kernels instead of being given them.

## Related courses

- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) is the prerequisite and every note here leans on it.
  [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] and [[Diagonalization]] feed the [[Spectral Theorem]];
  [[Dot Product]] and [[Basis]] feed [[Projection]] and [[Orthonormal Basis]];
  [[Matrix Inverse]] raises the "what if it is not square" question that [[Pseudoinverse]] answers;
  [[Kernel and Range]] and rank are what [[Low-Rank Approximation]] reduces.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234): **[[Least Squares]] here and [[Linear Regression]] there are the
  same object seen twice.** Statistics minimises the sum of squared residuals, this course projects
  onto a column space, and the equations are identical; $r^2$ is Pythagoras on the resulting right
  triangle. The covariance matrix [[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]] eigen-decomposes is built out
  of [[Variance]] and [[Correlation]], and Pearson's $r$ is the cosine of the angle between two
  centred data vectors, which is [[Inner Product]] and [[Projection]] again. [[Mean]] and
  [[Average Value]] are the shared vocabulary, and centring a data matrix is subtracting the column
  means.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200): [[Quadratic Form]] definiteness of the Hessian **is** the
  multivariable second-derivative test, which that course reaches from the
  [[Multivariable Calculus]] and [[Gradient]] side. Two routes to one criterion.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199): [[Orthonormal Basis]] here is the
  finite-dimensional case of [[Orthogonal Functions]] there, and a coordinate is a
  [[Fourier Coefficients|Fourier coefficient]] with the integral replaced by a sum. That course
  owns the [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] and the [[Fast Fourier Transform]]; this one owns
  [[Wavelet Transform]] and [[Image Processing]]. Its [[Convolution Theorem]] is why the filtering
  in [[Image Processing]] can be done in the frequency domain at all.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: [[Principal Component Analysis]] is what
  dimensionality reduction means, [[Vector Norm]] is where [[Loss Function|loss functions]] come
  from, and [[Gradient Descent]] minimises one of them over a surface whose local shape is a
  [[Quadratic Form]]. [[Image Processing]] is the classical half of [[Computer Vision]] and the
  designed-kernel ancestor of the [[CNN]].
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101): [[Inner Product]] adds structure to a [[Vector Space]] the way
  a ring adds structure to a [[Group]]. Same axiomatic move, different axioms.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: [[Gaussian Elimination]], [[Gram-Schmidt|QR]], and the SVD are
  the vault's numerical algorithms, all $O(n^3)$ for square inputs, and [[NumPy]]'s hundredfold
  vectorisation speedup is the cleanest example that [[Time Complexity]] is not the whole story.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]] (COMP 1631): the Python course. [[NumPy]] is the connection,
  and an `ndarray` is an [[Array]] with a shape.
